questions.question: Profit rose from ₹7.52 crore in FY24 to ₹27.01 crore in FY26, but only 52.5% of operating profit came in as cash. What does that suggest?

choices.text: The business is doing brilliantly; cash doesn't matter.
Some profit may be stuck in unpaid bills or unsold goods, so check how fast customers pay.
The company must have paid a big dividend.
Profit and cash are always equal, so the figures must be wrong.

questions.explanation: Profit is counted when a sale is made; cash arrives when the customer pays. For BLS Polymers Limited, only 52.5% of operating profit turned into cash, so money is getting stuck. Trade receivables and inventory are where to look.

questions.question: BLS Polymers Limited owes 0.56 rupees of loans for every rupee of its owners' money. Which is closest to the truth?

choices.text: Its loans are small to manageable next to what the owners have put in.
Its loans are heavy: lenders have more riding on it than its owners.
Loans never matter for a company that makes a profit.

questions.explanation: At 0.56 rupees of loans per rupee of owners' money, BLS Polymers Limited's owners have more in the business than its lenders.

questions.question: Insiders paid ₹2.90 a share on average. You would pay ₹150. What does the gap mean?

choices.text: Insiders got a much better deal, so be sure the business is worth your higher price.
The company will pay you back the difference.
The price band must be a mistake.

questions.explanation: At 51.7x what insiders paid, you pay a steep mark-up for BLS Polymers Limited: they gain far more than you can.
